9.2a — Hex, RGB & Data Abstraction

You have clicked colors in Unity a hundred times. Behind that picker is the exact place where binary becomes USEFUL: colors are bytes, written in hex, and the hex is just binary with better handwriting. Today you read the Inspector's secret language.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Hex = binary in groups of 4. One hex digit (0–9, A–F) covers exactly 4 bits: 0000=0 … 1111=F. A byte is therefore exactly TWO hex digits. Nobody reads 1111111111111111 when FF FF says the same thing out loud.

Dec0123456789101112131415
Hex0123456789ABCDEF
Bin0000000100100011010001010110011110001001101010111100110111101111

A color is four bytes. Unity's Color32 is R, G, B, A — one byte each, 0–255, so a color is literally a hex number like FF6600FF (full red, strong orange-green mix, no blue, full alpha). When you type new Color32(255, 102, 0, 255) you are writing FF6600FF in decimal cosplay:

// The site you are reading right now is themed blue:
// #6cb2ff → R=6c=108, G=b2=178, B=ff=255  → (108, 178, 255)

That IS your theme color, decoded by hand. The # in CSS means "hex follows," and web colors are 6 hex digits because web alpha is separate.

Socratic

The exam loves this: "how many colors can RGB represent?" Work it — 256 per channel, three channels — and say WHY the answer is 256³ (that is 9.1a's bits-to-range law, cubed). Then: why is 4 bits per channel (like old consoles) only 4096 colors — what did 8-bit color BUY?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — decode your game's palette. Pick three colors from your sprites/UI (use the eyedropper in the Sprite Editor or any color picker). For each, write the hex AND the decimal triple. Your cave should have a palette story — dark rock (low RGB values), bright coin (high R and G) — and now you can QUOTE it.

Step 2 — program a palette. Colors as data — the abstraction, in code:

public static class Palette
{
    //              name        hex        Color32
    public static readonly Color32 CAVE_ROCK = new Color32(0x4a, 0x4a, 0x55, 0xff);
    public static readonly Color32 COIN_GOLD = new Color32(0xff, 0xc4, 0x3d, 0xff);
    public static readonly Color32 DANGER    = new Color32(0xff, 0x33, 0x33, 0xff);
}

// your 8.3a hit flash, upgraded:
sr.color = new Color32(0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff); // white for 0.1s
// phase 3 boss tint:
sr.color = Palette.DANGER;

Why a palette class beats per-object color picking: change ONE line, the whole game's mood shifts. That is abstraction — the exam's word, in your repo.

Step 3 — the alpha byte. The fourth byte is transparency. 0xff = solid; 0x80 = half-visible (your hit flash could EASE from 0x80 to 0xff). Change your shockwave prefab's sprite alpha to 0x80 and note the readability change: transparent threats read as "avoidable" — alpha is communication, not decoration.

Bug Hunt: Byte bugs

  1. new Color32(300, 0, 0, 255) — what happens to the 300? (Bytes CLAMP or wrap — which one, and why is silent clamping a design risk?)
  2. 0x1F vs 0xF1 — a transposed hex pair. What color difference did that make? Why is hex the FASTEST way to catch a digit-swap bug in colors?
  3. Compute: how many bytes in a 1080p frame of RGBA data? (1920×1080×4 — do it on paper. Then ask: why does your GPU do this 60 times a second? That arithmetic explains why 9.7a needs a graphics pipeline.)
  4. The exam's classic: a 16-bit color system splits 5/6/5. Why does GREEN get the extra bit — and why do human eyes barely notice (look at your palette: which channel did you lean on?)
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Palette design

  1. Design a DANGER palette shift for your boss phases: phase 1 neutral, phase 2 warm, phase 3 red-shifted. Write the three hex codes BEFORE you look at them — then check the feel.
  2. AP practice: "A game represents a color as 3 bits — one per channel. How many colors?" Answer AND reason — then tell your neighbor why old-school games looked "chunky."
  3. Hard: your own Color32 parser — read a string like "FF6600" with int.Parse(s, NumberStyles.HexNumber). Which two lines of code does this save in a data-driven palette file?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Convert hex ↔ binary ↔ decimal for bytes, fast
  • Explain a color as four bytes and decode #RRGGBB by hand
  • Build a palette class as a data abstraction
  • Do the 256³ color-count argument from bits
